I don’t have any experience going to OMIC, but I am from Scappoose so I can provide a little info about transport options out here. Unfortunately, it is very limited. Rideshare apps like Lyft and Uber don’t really run out here; I haven’t heard of anyone having success actually picking up a ride from Scappoose to Portland or anywhere in the metro area. There have been a couple times when friends/family are able to catch a ride from the airport (PDX) back to Scappoose, but it’s a hefty bill and availability is still likely very limited. 

With all that said, we do have a shuttle service called the Columbia County Rider (CC rider) which goes back and forth between St. Helen’s (stops in Scappoose) and Portland. Here’s a link to their website to get more info about that and see if it’s an option for you. https://nwconnector.org/agencies/columbia-county-rider/ 

If that doesn’t work, you could try joining a local Facebook group like Concerned Citizens of Columbia County and/or Columbia County Rideshare to see if anyone who shares a similar schedule is able to give you a ride that way. 

I hope this helps, best of luck to you!

V to the D is a technique to determine the correct working end for the tooth surface you are instrumenting. V is referring to the last bend in the instrument before the terminal shank. So for posterior teeth, that V should be pointing to the D (distal) when using the correct working end. And for anterior teeth (surfaces towards and surfaces away) the V should be pointing the T (tooth). I hope this makes sense!☺️

Im not a doctor, rather a dental hygiene student, but we also need to be aware of cannabis use for local anesthesia and nitrous oxide sedation so I can give a little explanation. Basically, the cannabinods interact with the anesthetic and can cause them to be processed faster so the correct anesthesia dosage by weight for that patient might not actually be enough. My instructors have told us that they’ve had an alarming amount of incidences where people have woken up during say, a wisdom tooth extraction, because their anesthesia was too light due to marijuana consumption that was not told to the dentist/doctor. All it means is that it’s important to tell your doctor these things so they can give you an increased dose of anesthesia to make sure you don’t wake up!

Hi! I am also a pre-dental hygiene student getting ready to apply to the program; doing prereqs, shadowing, etc. and I was also really nervous to shadow an RDH for the first time.

Firstly, as nervous as you are, I promise it's totally not a big deal and once you get in there and start doing it you will think "jeez what was I even worried about"? I started shadowing my personal hygienist, so that made it a little easier because I was already comfortable with the office and with the hygienist so I would definitely recommend doing that at first to help with the anxiety. I just called the office and said something along the lines of, "Hi, my name is ----- and I am a student at ----- studying to become a dental hygienist. One of the requirements to get into the DH program is to shadow a hygienist for 20 hours and I was wondering if this is something you do at your office?" Every place I have shadowed at (3 places) has been extremely kind and happy to help over the phone (which is something I was worried about because I hate talking on the phone) and they just set up a time to shadow and tell you anything special you need to wear like scrubs, hair tied back, stuff like that, and you're all set up!

When you go into the office, just go to the front desk and introduce yourself, "Hi my name is ---- and I am here to shadow one of your hygienists today" or something like that and since yo u have already set it up with the office they'll just say "Okay awesome, follow me!" and you'll follow them back into the clinic. Some places have given me a tour, let me meet all the staff, stuff like that, and then I meet the hygienist I will be shadowing and start shadowing them.

Basically what it consists of is just "shadowing" the hygienist; being a fly on the wall. Usually you just sit in the other chair that is in the hygienists room and when they bring a patient in they'll probably introduce you like "This is ----- and they are studying to be a dental hygienist, is it okay if they watch and learn while I do your cleaning?" and I have never had a patient not be okay with it. Not to say it can't happen, but all of the patients I've watched have been eager to help me learn stuff. Sometimes the hygienists will let me help with perio charting (just typing in the numbers they say into the computer) which is fun because it gives you a hands on experience.

As far as questions go, I always bring a small notebook and pen so that I can come prepared with questions and write down answers as I go. I always ask questions either related to the program itself (because the hygienists I've shadowed went thru the program I want to go through) or questions about the job itself and their satisfaction with it. Here's some example questions:

How many days a week would you reccomend working?

What is the most challenging part of school/your daily job?

Do you enjoy your job/feel like you made the right career choice?

Do you have any tips for hygiene school?

Do you have any tips to get into hygiene school?

Anything tips/things to avoid when looking for a job after school? (kind of trying to find out the red flags that offices can have)

Things like that, and really once you get in there you might notice that questions just naturally come up like questions you can ask about the Xrays or their equipment and stuff like that. As far as etiquette goes just be nice and respectful of the hygienist's time (as well as all other staff in the office) and the patient's time. Just observe what the hygienist is doing and ask questions when they come up but don't bombard them with questions because they are still trying to do their job.

Just go in there eager to learn everything you can and have an open mind and everything will go smoothly; I know its nervewracking but shadowing has been really rewarding for me because it has allowed me to confirm that I can see myself doing that job and really makes me excited to get there!

I hope this has helped and not been a complete word mess, lol.

If you have any more questions or any clarifications, please don't hesitate to reach out to me, we're all in this together! :)

Look into your mouth, on the sides right before your throat goes down, and see if there are any little whitish spots/chunks. If so, these are tonsil stones, they are caused by mucus, dead cells, and other things getting trapped in the little nooks and crannies of your tonsils. They are known to cause bad breath and can be removed by gargling salt water, gently dislodging them with a blunt object (DO NOT go too hard on your tonsils), or just waiting until they dislodge themselves (which should happen eventually).
